MARITAL SUMMARY DISSOLUTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Marital Summary Dissolution — Information Sheet concerns the marriage of Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, who were married on June 14, 2020 and identify March 2, 2026 as their date of separation. It is prepared for background use in connection with the possible filing of a joint petition for summary dissolution of marriage under Family Code §§ 2400-2406 in the Superior Court of California, County of Sacramento County, or, if the eligibility conditions described in this document are not met, an ordinary petition for dissolution of marriage in the same court. This information sheet describes California's summary dissolution procedure — its narrow eligibility conditions, the joint-petition process, the right to revoke before judgment, and the effect and limited set-aside grounds of the eventual judgment — as background for that filing. It is not itself a joint petition or any other court filing, and completing it does not dissolve, terminate, or otherwise change the marital status of Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee. Only a court judgment of dissolution can do that.

ELIGIBILITY CONDITIONS FOR SUMMARY DISSOLUTION
California law allows a marriage to be dissolved through the summary dissolution procedure only if all of the following conditions exist at the time the proceeding is commenced: either party independently meets the same jurisdictional (residency) requirements that apply to an ordinary dissolution of marriage; irreconcilable differences have caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage and it should be dissolved; there are no children of the relationship born before or during the marriage or adopted by the parties during the marriage, and neither party, to that party's knowledge, is pregnant; the marriage is not more than five years in duration as of the date of separation; neither party has any interest in real property wherever located, apart from a narrow lease exception — a residential lease occupied by either party that includes no purchase option and terminates within one year of the date the petition is filed; unpaid obligations incurred by either or both parties after the date of marriage, excluding any obligation relating to an automobile, do not exceed the statutory dollar threshold, stated in the statute's current codified text as four thousand dollars ($4,000); the total fair market value of community property assets — excluding all encumbrances and automobiles, but including any deferred compensation or retirement plan — is less than the statutory dollar threshold, stated in the statute's current codified text as twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), and neither party's separate property assets (subject to the same exclusions) exceed that same $25,000 figure; the parties have executed an agreement dividing their community assets and liabilities, along with any documents, title certificates, bills of sale, or other transfer paperwork needed to carry it out; the parties waive any right to spousal support from each other; the parties irrevocably waive their respective rights to appeal and to move for a new trial upon entry of the judgment; the parties have read and understand the summary dissolution brochure that the statute requires each superior court to make available; and the parties desire that the court dissolve the marriage. The $4,000 and $25,000 figures printed in the statute's own text are not fixed permanently: the statute separately directs that the unpaid-obligations figure be adjusted for changes in the value of the dollar on January 1 of every odd-numbered year beginning in 1985, and that the community/separate-property figure be adjusted the same way beginning in 1993, with the adjustments computed and published by the Judicial Council rather than written into the statute's text itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) A marriage may be dissolved by the summary dissolution procedure provided in this chapter if all of the following conditions exist at the time the proceeding is commenced: (1) Either party has met the jurisdictional requirements of Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 2320) with regard to dissolution of marriage. (2) Irreconcilable differences have caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage and the marriage should be dissolved. (3) There are no children of the relationship of the parties born before or during the marriage or adopted by the parties during the marriage, and neither party, to that party’s knowledge, is pregnant. (4) The marriage is not more than five years in duration as of the date of separation of the parties. (5) Neither party has any interest in real property wherever situated, with the exception of the lease of a residence occupied by either party which satisfies the following requirements: (A) The lease does not include an option to purchase. (B) The lease terminates within one year from the date of the filing of the petition. (6) There are no unpaid obligations in excess of four thousand dollars ($4,000) incurred by either or both of the parties after the date of their marriage, excluding the amount of any unpaid obligation with respect to an automobile. (7) The total fair market value of community property assets, excluding all encumbrances and automobiles, including any deferred compensation or retirement plan, is less than twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), and neither party has separate property assets, excluding all encumbrances and automobiles, in excess of twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000). (8) The parties have executed an agreement setting forth the division of assets and the assumption of liabilities of the community, and have executed any documents, title certificates, bills of sale, or other evidence of transfer necessary to effectuate the agreement. (9) The parties waive any rights to spousal support. (10) The parties, upon entry of the judgment of dissolution of marriage pursuant to Section 2403, irrevocably waive their respective rights to appeal and their rights to move for a new trial. (11) The parties have read and understand the summary dissolution brochure provided for in Section 2406. (12) The parties desire that the court dissolve the marriage. (b) On January 1, 1985, and on January 1 of each odd-numbered year thereafter, the amounts in paragraph (6) of subdivision (a) shall be adjusted to reflect any change in the value of the dollar. On January 1, 1993, and on January 1 of each odd-numbered year thereafter, the amounts in paragraph (7) of subdivision (a) shall be adjusted to reflect any change in the value of the dollar. The adjustments shall be made by multiplying the base amounts by the percentage change in the California Consumer Price Index as compiled by the Department of Industrial Relations, with the result rounded to the nearest thousand dollars. The Judicial Council shall compute and publish the amounts."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2400(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the twelve conditions for summary dissolution and the mechanism for periodically adjusting the dollar thresholds (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2400.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for summary dissolution of a marriage — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific marriage. This document is informational only: it does not itself dissolve any marriage or determine eligibility, grounds, or property/debt values for any specific case; only a court judgment does that. This clause cites a single statutory section with two subsections (§ 2400(a) and § 2400(b)); both are quoted because they state distinct rules (the twelve eligibility conditions, and the mechanism for periodically adjusting two of the dollar figures those conditions use) — this is not two independent sources. The $4,000 and $25,000 figures quoted here are the amounts printed in the statute's own currently codified text (last amended effective January 1, 2015); because subdivision (b) requires the Judicial Council to compute and publish inflation-adjusted current versions of those two figures outside the statute's own text, the actually-applicable current dollar thresholds may differ from $4,000 and $25,000, and this document's research did not independently locate or verify any Judicial Council publication stating the present adjusted amounts.

COMMENCING THE PROCEEDING: THE JOINT PETITION
A summary dissolution proceeding is commenced by filing a joint petition for summary dissolution, in the form prescribed by the Judicial Council. The petition must be signed under oath by both spouses, and must include a statement that, as of the date the joint petition is filed, all of the eligibility conditions described elsewhere in this document have been met; the mailing address of each spouse; and a statement of whether either spouse elects to have a former name restored and, if so, what name. Unlike an ordinary dissolution proceeding, which one spouse alone may commence by petition, the summary dissolution procedure requires both spouses to jointly sign and file the same petition from the outset.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) A proceeding for summary dissolution of the marriage shall be commenced by filing a joint petition for summary dissolution in the form prescribed by the Judicial Council. (b) The petition shall be signed under oath by both spouses and shall include all of the following: (1) A statement that as of the date of the filing of the joint petition all of the conditions set forth in Section 2400 have been met. (2) The mailing address of each spouse. (3) A statement whether a spouse elects to have their former name restored and, if so, the name to be restored."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2401(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the joint petition requirement and its required contents (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2401.)

This document is informational only: it does not itself commence any proceeding or dissolve any marriage. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 2401); no additional independent source was located for it.

RIGHT TO REVOKE THE JOINT PETITION BEFORE JUDGMENT
At any time before an application for judgment is filed, either party to the marriage may revoke the joint petition for summary dissolution — acting alone, without the other party's agreement — which terminates the summary dissolution proceeding. Revocation is accomplished by filing a notice of revocation, in the form prescribed by the Judicial Council, with the clerk of the court where the proceeding was commenced. The revoking party must send a copy of the notice of revocation to the other party by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to that party's last known address.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) At any time before the filing of application for judgment pursuant to Section 2403, either party to the marriage may revoke the joint petition for summary dissolution and thereby terminate the summary dissolution proceeding filed pursuant to this chapter. (b) The revocation shall be effected by filing with the clerk of the court where the proceeding was commenced a notice of revocation in a form and content as shall be prescribed by the Judicial Council. (c) The revoking party shall send a copy of the notice of revocation to the other party by first-class mail, postage prepaid, at the other party’s last known address."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2402(a)-(c) (California Legislative Information text), the right to revoke the joint petition before judgment and how revocation is made (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2402.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for summary dissolution of a marriage — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific marriage. This document is informational only: it does not itself revoke any petition or affect any pending proceeding. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 2402); no additional independent source was located for it.

SIX-MONTH WAIT AND ENTRY OF JUDGMENT
Once six months have expired from the date the joint petition for summary dissolution was filed, the court is required to enter a judgment dissolving the marriage, unless a revocation has been filed before then. Entry of the judgment restores both parties to the status of single persons, and either party may marry after the judgment is entered. The court clerk is required to send a notice of entry of judgment to each party at that party's last known address.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "When six months have expired from the date of the filing of the joint petition for summary dissolution, the court shall, unless a revocation has been filed pursuant to Section 2402, enter the judgment dissolving the marriage. The judgment restores to the parties the status of single persons, and either party may marry after the entry of the judgment. The clerk shall send a notice of entry of judgment to each of the parties at the party’s last known address."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2403 (California Legislative Information text), the six-month wait, entry of judgment, and restoration of single status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2403.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for summary dissolution of a marriage — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific marriage. This document is informational only: it does not itself enter any judgment or dissolve any marriage; only a court judgment does that. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 2403); no additional independent source was located for it.

EFFECT OF THE JUDGMENT AND THE STATUTORY RIGHT TO SEEK TO SET IT ASIDE
Entry of the judgment operates as a final adjudication of the parties' rights and obligations regarding both the status of the marriage and their property rights, and it constitutes a waiver of each party's rights to spousal support, to appeal, and to move for a new trial. That finality is not absolute: the statute separately preserves the right of either party to bring an action to set the judgment aside for fraud, duress, accident, mistake, or another ground recognized at law or in equity, or to bring a motion under Code of Civil Procedure § 473. If either party proves that the parties did not actually meet the eligibility conditions at the time the petition was filed, the court is required to set the judgment aside as to every matter except the dissolved status of the marriage itself — meaning the marital status the judgment established remains intact even where the judgment is otherwise set aside on that ground.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Entry of the judgment pursuant to Section 2403 constitutes: (a) A final adjudication of the rights and obligations of the parties with respect to the status of the marriage and property rights. (b) A waiver of their respective rights to spousal support, rights to appeal, and rights to move for a new trial."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2404 (California Legislative Information text), the judgment's effect as a final adjudication and a waiver of support, appeal, and new-trial rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2404.)
  "(a) Entry of the judgment pursuant to Section 2403 does not prejudice nor bar the rights of either of the parties to institute an action to set aside the judgment for fraud, duress, accident, mistake, or other grounds recognized at law or in equity or to make a motion pursuant to Section 473 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (b) The court shall set aside a judgment entered pursuant to Section 2403 regarding all matters except the status of the marriage, upon proof that the parties did not meet the requirements of Section 2400 at the time the petition was filed."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2405(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory grounds and scope for setting the judgment aside (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2405.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for summary dissolution of a marriage — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific marriage. This document is informational only: it does not itself adjudicate any rights, waive any right on behalf of any party, or set aside any judgment. This clause cites two separately and independently numbered statutory sections (§ 2404 and § 2405) that address distinct subjects — the effect of the judgment, and the statutory grounds and scope for setting it aside — so, unlike the other authority clauses in this document, this one rests on two genuinely independent sections rather than subsections of a single section.

HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE CORPUS'S DOMESTIC PARTNERSHIP ADMINISTRATIVE TERMINATION
The summary dissolution procedure addressed in this document is available only to married spouses, and only through a court proceeding: eligibility depends on a party independently meeting the same jurisdictional (residency) requirements that apply to an ordinary marital dissolution, and the proceeding is commenced by filing a joint petition with the superior court, which itself enters the eventual judgment. That is a different mechanism from the one described in this corpus's Domestic Partnership Dissolution — Information Sheet, under which a registered domestic partnership meeting a separately defined set of statutory conditions can be terminated without any court proceeding at all, simply by filing a Notice of Termination directly with the Secretary of State. The two mechanisms share a family resemblance in their numeric eligibility conditions — both use a duration cap on the relationship, dollar thresholds tied to Family Code § 2400 for debts and property, and a similar real-property/lease exception — but they are codified in different parts of the Family Code, apply to a different legal status (marriage, as opposed to a registered domestic partnership), and are decided by different government actors: a superior court judgment for summary dissolution of a marriage, as opposed to the Secretary of State's administrative processing of a Notice of Termination for a domestic partnership.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Either party has met the jurisdictional requirements of Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 2320) with regard to dissolution of marriage."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2400(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), summary dissolution requires the same jurisdictional (residency) requirements that apply to an ordinary court dissolution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2400.)
  "A proceeding for summary dissolution of the marriage shall be commenced by filing a joint petition for summary dissolution in the form prescribed by the Judicial Council."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2401(a) (California Legislative Information text), summary dissolution of a marriage is commenced by filing a joint petition, a court filing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2401.)
  "A registered domestic partnership may be terminated without filing a proceeding for dissolution of domestic partnership by the filing of a Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State pursuant to this section, provided that all of the following conditions exist at the time of the filing:"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 299(a) (California Legislative Information text; quoted as already verified in this corpus's dpdissolution_administrative_notice_eligibility clause), administrative termination of a domestic partnership instead proceeds by a Secretary of State filing, without any dissolution proceeding (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=299.)

This document is informational only: it does not itself dissolve any marriage or terminate any partnership. The § 2400(a)(1) and § 2401(a) text quoted here is the same text already quoted in full in this document's summarydissolution_eligibility_conditions and summarydissolution_petition_commencement_and_contents clauses, reused here only to support the contrast drawn in this clause's body, not as an additional independent source. The § 299(a) text quoted here is not independently re-fetched or re-verified by this document's research; it is reused, verbatim, from this corpus's existing, separately verified dpdissolution_administrative_notice_eligibility clause (checked 2026-09-02) in the Domestic Partnership Dissolution — Information Sheet document. The two statutory schemes being contrasted — Family Code §§ 2400-2406 (Division 6, Part 3, Chapter 5) and Family Code § 299 (a different division and part of the Family Code governing registered domestic partnerships) — are genuinely separate, independently numbered statutory provisions, so the underlying subject-matter contrast this clause draws is not undermined by reusing already-quoted text to state each side of it.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — NOT A COURT FILING
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________

Signature of Morgan Casey Lee: ☐ _________________________

It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not dissolve a marriage, establish eligibility for summary dissolution, or determine grounds for any specific case; only a court judgment of dissolution can dissolve a marriage.]
